# Contracts, notaries and merchant courts (`commercial_law_contract_enforcement`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, written_law_code, standard_weights_measures
- Core idea: Long-distance trade needs a way to make a stranger keep his word. The proven package: a written contract, witnessed and sealed or registered with a public notary whose record counts as proof; a merchant court that judges fast by the custom of traders, with merchants as judges; and a community that shuts out a proven cheat everywhere its members trade. The threat of losing all future business makes honesty pay even where no state can reach. Add an agent's duty to keep accounts and joint responsibility of a town for its merchants' debts, and credit can travel across borders.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming trade needs a strong state first: Old Assyrian, Maghribi and Hanseatic traders enforced contracts through their own communities and reputation
  - Ordinary courts are too slow and formal for travelling merchants: fair courts settled cases between tides or before the fair closed
  - Oral agreements between distant partners cannot be proved after one of them dies; write, witness and keep duplicates
  - Reputation networks work only inside a closed group, which then excludes outsiders and resists newcomers
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1900 BC – Old Assyrian merchants at Kanesh (Anatolia) use sealed tablets, witnesses, partnership contracts and their own colony court; some 23,000 tablets survive; greece: 4th c. BC – Athens creates fast monthly maritime suits (dikai emporikai) open to foreigners, requiring a written contract; rome: ius gentium and the peregrine praetor (242 BC) for cases involving foreigners; the Rhodian sea law on jettison; india: guild (shreni) rules recognised as binding law in dharma texts and the Arthashastra; china: Tang (7th–9th c.) – written sale and loan contracts with guarantors and witnesses, preserved at Turfan and Dunhuang; islamic: 7th c. – Quran 2:282 orders debts to be written and witnessed; 11th c. Maghribi Jewish traders of the Cairo Geniza police agents through reputation; europe: 12th c. – Italian public notaries (Genoa registers from 1154); 12th–13th c. Champagne fair courts and law merchant; 1283 Consulate of the Sea in Valencia
- Read:
  - Avner Greif, Institutions and the Path to the Modern Economy (2006)
  - Mogens Trolle Larsen, Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia (2015)
